title: INSERT
description: Add accepted rows with explicit target roles, preserve the retained employee insertion checker, and distinguish input values, defaults, statement failure and transaction completion.
notes:
## Insertion creates new accepted rows

INSERT adds rows to an existing table under its definition and applicable access rules. It does not create the table or update an arbitrary row that happens to share a name. A campus service might insert a newly accepted employee or request. The starting schema determines which roles must be supplied and which values the database may generate or initialize.

The retained introductory task adds employee 9, Farah, with a specified department and salary. Those values are requirements, not suggestions to reinterpret from another row. Existing employees must remain intact. A solution that deletes the table and recreates only the example output would not implement the requested state transition even if a displayed result happened to look similar.

## Name target columns explicitly

INSERT INTO employees(id,name,department,salary) states the destination roles before supplying their values. The value order follows that explicit list. If the list names name before id, the values must follow that changed order. Match each value to its intended role rather than assume the physical column order or the spelling of a literal will correct a mistake.

An explicit list reduces dependence on unrelated table-column reordering and permits deliberate omission of generated or defaulted properties. It does not make the statement immune to every schema change. Renaming a referenced column, narrowing a type or changing an accepted-domain rule can still break it. Describe the practical compatibility advantage precisely rather than promise universal future-proofing.

```sql
INSERT INTO employees (id, name, department, salary)
VALUES (9, 'Farah', 'Engineering', 75000);
```

## Literal values need the right representation

Numeric and string values have different syntax. A quoted name is text, while salary is an integer in this simplified exercise. An apostrophe inside a literal requires the target's correct escaping rules. In application code, supported parameter binding is the appropriate way to supply untrusted values rather than concatenate them into SQL text.

Parameters for values do not automatically substitute arbitrary identifiers such as table names. If an application genuinely chooses a target dynamically, it needs an explicit supported identifier policy. The lab uses fixed known tables, so its reference statements do not require dynamic object selection or privileged access beyond the isolated operation being tested.

## Omission is different from explicit missing input

A column omitted from the INSERT list can use its supported default or generation rule. A nullable property can also remain absent under its definition. An explicitly supplied NULL is another input and may be rejected by a required-value rule instead of invoking the default. Read the target's exact definitions and statement behaviour before deciding what omission means.

The second task inserts a new request while omitting status so the declared pending policy applies. It preserves existing statuses rather than update old rows to the default. That distinction is important: initialization describes a newly inserted fact, whereas a backfill is a separate modification of existing accepted state.

## Constraints remain the trusted acceptance boundary

A primary key rejects duplicate identity, a unique rule protects its intended value combination, NOT NULL requires recorded presence under the configured rules, CHECK restricts a supported domain and FOREIGN KEY protects a supported reference. A row must satisfy the relevant enforced contract. Knowing that one supplied value looks plausible is not enough.

If a required ordinary property has no accepted supplied value or usable default, the insert needs to be handled according to the actual engine's strictness and conversion rules. These fixtures use strict ordinary-column settings where rejected missing input is part of the assessment. Do not turn a configured error expectation into an unqualified claim about every permissive mode and special column type.

## Statement failure and transaction failure are different scopes

For an ordinary transactional InnoDB INSERT without conflict-altering variants, a constraint failure can reject the statement's affected row changes. That is not identical to proving an entire surrounding application transaction has been undone automatically. Earlier statements, client error handling and engine semantics determine what state remains and what recovery is required.

Other storage engines and variants such as IGNORE or a defined duplicate-key update can have different accepted outcomes. The basic exercise uses an ordinary insert so the intended boundary is visible. Do not add those variants merely to hide an unexpected duplicate or missing property; they change the contract and belong to an explicit conflict-handling policy.

## Insertion can invoke additional database behaviour

Defaults, generated values, supported triggers and reference actions can contribute to the resulting state. A trigger's effects are not obvious solely from the visible VALUES list. Inspect the relevant definition when predicting an insert's outcome rather than assume the statement affects only the literal cells shown in a tutorial.

That does not make triggers an authorization shortcut. The caller still needs the permitted operation under trusted access rules, and any privileged logic has its own reviewed boundary. The isolated tasks do not create application triggers or claim that a successful synthetic insert proves an account is allowed to write every production employee record.

## A repeated attempt needs a deliberate identity policy

The retained task guarantees employee 9 is absent initially. Running its ordinary INSERT again against the changed state would encounter the primary key rather than silently replace Farah. That is expected identity protection, not proof the first insertion failed. A retry policy must decide whether the same request should return an existing result or report a conflict.

Do not assume every insert is naturally idempotent. A generated surrogate key can create a second business record on retry, while a fixed accepted key can reject it. Business request identity and conflict handling need their own design. The task remains a precise one-time transition, with duplicate rejection checked separately rather than suppressed.

## Query-sourced insertion still needs a destination contract

INSERT can take rows from a SELECT instead of a literal VALUES list. The second exercise uses one supplied proposed request so hidden fixtures can vary its identity and label. The target list names request_id and label, and status is deliberately omitted. This introduces a source contract without changing the rule that the accepted destination definition governs the write.

A source query can return zero or several rows unless the problem states otherwise. Here exactly one proposed_request row is guaranteed. Do not invent a dummy request when that condition is not met in another task, and do not select an arbitrary row to hide an unexpected population. The source cardinality is part of the assessment's stated preconditions.

## Verification reads the full intended post-state

The retained employee checker runs after the student's statement and selects all employees in id order. It verifies both the new required row and preservation of earlier rows. Keeping the checker unchanged maintains the original assessment contract. Adding a second unsolicited result set to the submitted SQL could interfere with output comparison, so the reference submission contains the write only.

Hidden fixtures vary the existing employees while preserving the requested Farah row. An empty starting table still permits the same insertion. A negative duplicate-key case confirms employee 9 cannot be inserted again under the primary rule. These are meaningful boundaries, rather than multiple sample outputs that only rename the same unchanged table.

## Insertion acknowledgment is not every downstream success

A database accepting the statement is narrower than an application completing an entire workflow. A surrounding transaction may still fail, a later dependent operation may reject its state, or an external service may have its own result. Confirm the authoritative boundary relevant to the user rather than assume a generated id or one statement acknowledgment establishes every later action.

The exercises remain local table transitions, with deterministic reads and explicit expected rows. They do not perform production deployment, contact other users or alter application authorization. Keeping those boundaries clear lets the content explain the write accurately without pretending a classroom insertion is an operationally complete hiring or registration process.

## Report the values, preserved state and evidence

A useful illustration traces starting rows, the submitted addition and the checker observation. The notes, MCQs and reference statement should agree on exact column roles and defaults. Then students can explain why the new row appears, why old rows remain and why a repeated protected identity is rejected.

Recorded MariaDB compatibility execution verifies these synthetic inserts and selected rejected writes. Exact MySQL/provider behaviour, untested trigger effects, concurrency policies and application migration application remain separate checks. The prepared content package is complete without claiming instructional employee writes happened in production or that explicit column lists protect against every possible future schema change.

questions.question_text: What does an INSERT statement add to an existing table?
options: New rows under the table’s applicable acceptance rules
Removes a row from a table
questions.explanation: The statement can insert one or several rows; it does not define the table itself.

questions.question_text: Why explicitly name target columns?
options: It is required syntax with no alternative
It states value roles, reduces dependence on physical ordering and permits deliberate omission
It makes the INSERT run faster
Named columns are mandatory for NOT NULL columns only
questions.explanation: It does not guarantee compatibility with every later schema change.

questions.question_text: Why must missing required input be evaluated under the actual target settings?
options: The column is set to an empty string automatically
Defaults, strictness and special column rules determine the supported error or conversion outcome
The column is set to zero
questions.explanation: The fixtures use strict ordinary-column rejection rather than a universal permissive-mode claim.

questions.question_text: For an ordinary transactional InnoDB insert without IGNORE or an update variant, what does a uniqueness failure imply?
options: Only the violating value is skipped; the rest proceeds
The statement is rejected under its transactional rules rather than accepting an arbitrary partial successful insert
The row is inserted with a NULL instead
questions.explanation: Surrounding transaction recovery and nontransactional engines need separate treatment.

questions.question_text: Is `INSERT INTO employees VALUES (9, 'Farah', 'Engineering', 75000)` (no column list) as robust as naming columns explicitly?
options: No — it relies on positional order matching the table's current column order, which can break if the schema changes
It is more robust because it's shorter
questions.explanation: Omitting the column list ties the statement to the table's exact current column order — a fragile assumption.

questions.question_text: Can an INSERT trigger additional automatic behavior beyond adding the row?
options: No, INSERT only ever does exactly what's written
Yes — an INSERT trigger (Chapter 30) can fire automatically as a side effect
Only DELETE statements can have triggers
Triggers only fire on SELECT statements
questions.explanation: Triggers can attach extra automatic behavior to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

questions.question_text: Which constraint types can cause an INSERT to fail?
options: UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, and PRIMARY KEY constraints can all reject an INSERT that violates them
Constraints never affect INSERT, only UPDATE
questions.explanation: Any violated constraint on the table can cause the INSERT to be rejected.

questions.question_text: What is the relationship between INSERT and the rest of DML (UPDATE, DELETE)?
options: INSERT is the entry point that creates rows which UPDATE and DELETE later modify or remove
INSERT can only be used after a DELETE
UPDATE and DELETE must always precede any INSERT
questions.explanation: INSERT creates the data that subsequent UPDATE/DELETE statements act upon.

questions.question_text: Does INSERT define a missing target table?
options: Only if it has a key
questions.explanation: The destination definition is a prerequisite.

questions.question_text: What happens to the retained task’s old employees?
options: They remain while Farah is added
questions.explanation: The requested transition is additive.

questions.question_text: Which input can request pending through omission?
options: An insert that names request_id and label but omits status
questions.explanation: The target definition supplies the omitted initialization policy.

questions.question_text: Does a named target list protect every possible schema change?
questions.explanation: Referenced names and accepted domains can still change.

questions.question_text: What should application code use for untrusted value inputs?
questions.explanation: Value representation must preserve the trusted boundary.

questions.question_text: Does a value parameter automatically select arbitrary table identifiers?
questions.explanation: Identifiers require a separately supported policy.

questions.question_text: Why keep a trailing checker after the submitted write?
options: It must create the old table later
It observes the actual post-insert state
questions.explanation: Execution order is part of the retained assessment.

questions.question_text: Is ordinary INSERT automatically idempotent?
questions.explanation: Retry and business identity need a policy.

questions.question_text: Why not silently add IGNORE to a duplicate failure?
options: It changes the accepted outcome rather than explaining the conflict
It preserves every ordinary error identically
questions.explanation: Conflict variants need explicit requirements.

questions.question_text: Does one insert acknowledgment prove a surrounding workflow committed?
options: Only if it returns an id
questions.explanation: Later transaction or application steps can still fail.

questions.question_text: Why select all employees in the checker?
options: To verify the addition and preservation of supplied old rows
questions.explanation: The full postcondition includes unchanged earlier state.

questions.question_text: What remains outside these local fixtures?
options: Exact provider, untested triggers and production workflow behaviour
questions.explanation: Evidence stays attached to the actual executed scope.

coding_problems.title: Insert a New Employee
coding_problems.original_check_sql: SELECT id, name, department, salary FROM employees ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.check_sql: SELECT id, name, department, salary FROM employees ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.task: Insert employee id=9,name Farah,department Engineering,salary 75000 using an explicit target column list. Preserve all supplied employees. Id 9 is initially absent. The retained trailing checker reads the full result; submit the write without an extra result set.
coding_problems.expected:
id	name	department	salary
1	Asha	Engineering	85000
2	Rohan	Sales	62000
9	Farah	Engineering	75000
coding_problems.ordering: The retained checker orders by id.
constraints: Original identity, setup and checker preserved.
A one-time ordinary insertion; do not overwrite earlier employees.
edge_cases: An empty starting population still receives Farah.
Repeated attempt at id 9 is rejected by the key.
hints: The checker reads the result after your statement.
coding_problems.explanation: The exact new row is added while the original post-write checker verifies all preserved and newly inserted records.

validation_cases.seed_sql:

validation_cases.expected:

9	Farah	Engineering	75000

coding_problems.title: Add a supplied request while preserving future-default semantics
coding_problems.task: Exactly one proposed_request row supplies a new request_id and label. Insert it into requests using those roles only so the declared status default supplies pending. Existing and new ids do not overlap. Preserve earlier statuses, then return request_id,label,status.
coding_problems.schema_sql: SET SESSION sql_mode='STRICT_ALL_TABLES'; CREATE TABLE requests (request_id INT PRIMARY KEY,label VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'); CREATE TABLE proposed_request (request_id INT PRIMARY KEY,label VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO requests VALUES (1,'Old','held'); INSERT INTO proposed_request VALUES (9,'New');
coding_problems.expected:
request_id	label	status
1	Old	held
9	New	pending
constraints: Exactly one supplied proposal in each fixture.
No status backfill or default change.
edge_cases: An initially empty requests table is permitted.
hints: Use the supplied proposal as the value source.
Leave status out of the insert target list.
coding_problems.solution_sql: INSERT INTO requests (request_id,label) SELECT request_id,label FROM proposed_request; SELECT request_id,label,status FROM requests ORDER BY request_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Explicit target roles preserve the new input while the database supplies only the intended omitted initialization value.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO requests VALUES (3,'Earlier','active'); INSERT INTO proposed_request VALUES (8,'Next');
validation_cases.expected:
request_id	label	status
3	Earlier	active
8	Next	pending

original_questions.question_text: What does the INSERT statement do?
options: Adds a new row to a table
Removes a row from a table
original_questions.explanation: INSERT is specifically for adding new rows.

original_questions.question_text: Why is explicitly naming columns in INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...) considered best practice?
options: It is required syntax with no alternative
It makes the statement immune to breaking if the table's column order changes later, and allows omitting columns with defaults
It makes the INSERT run faster
Named columns are mandatory for NOT NULL columns only
original_questions.explanation: Explicit column lists are robust to schema evolution and let you skip columns that don't need a value.

original_questions.question_text: What happens if you omit a NOT NULL column with no DEFAULT from an INSERT?
options: The column is set to an empty string automatically
The column is set to zero
original_questions.explanation: A NOT NULL column with no default requires an explicit value; omitting it fails the insert by design.

original_questions.question_text: If a single VALUES row violates a UNIQUE constraint, what happens to the rest of that INSERT statement?
options: Only the violating value is skipped; the rest proceeds
The entire statement fails — no partial insert happens for that statement
The row is inserted with a NULL instead
original_questions.explanation: A constraint violation rejects the whole statement it occurred in.

original_questions.question_text: Is `INSERT INTO employees VALUES (9, 'Farah', 'Engineering', 75000)` (no column list) as robust as naming columns explicitly?

It is more robust because it's shorter
original_questions.explanation: Omitting the column list ties the statement to the table's exact current column order — a fragile assumption.
